lessons.title: A 20-Point Governance Checklist for Indian Stocks

body.text: A checklist does not make you right. It makes you consistent, and consistency is what stops a good story from overriding a bad filing.

children.text: You now have every individual skill this course set out to teach: reading shareholding patterns and pledges, mapping group structures, judging boards and auditors, sizing related party leakage, scoring capital allocation, testing earnings quality, and pulling a regulatory file. This lesson turns all of it into one repeatable process, so that you apply the same standard to a stock you already love as to one you have never heard of.

Score each of the 20 checks as 0, 1, or 2. Two means clearly strong, one means acceptable or mixed, zero means a genuine concern. The maximum is 40. Write one line of evidence next to every score, with the document you took it from, so you can compare with last year and with peers rather than relying on memory.

stats.label: 32 to 40
stats.context: Governance is an asset; normal position sizing

stats.label: 24 to 31
stats.context: Invest with specific items on a watchlist and review each quarter

stats.label: 16 to 23
stats.context: Only with a large margin of safety and a smaller position

stats.label: Below 16
stats.context: No valuation compensates for this many failures at once

body.text: Some findings override the total score. Treat these as red lines: an adverse opinion or disclaimer of opinion from the auditor; an auditor resigning because information or evidence was not provided; a subsisting regulatory order restraining promoters or key executives from boards or the securities market; related party loans and guarantees above 25% of net worth; or a promoter pledge above half the promoter holding that is still rising. Any one of these means no, regardless of how the other 19 items score.

children.text: Section A: Ownership and Control (Checks 1 to 5)

cells: Promoter holding level and five-year trend, measured in share count
Shareholding pattern on BSE or NSE; screener.in
Stable or rising through genuine purchases
Steady unexplained selling, or a stake falling while management calls the stock cheap
Promoter pledge: level, trend, and stated reason
Pledged percentage on screener.in; encumbrance filings
No pledge, or small and falling
Pledge rising as the share price falls, funding unlisted group businesses
Group structure complexity
Form AOC-1; related party note
Few subsidiaries, each with a clear purpose
Dozens of entities, offshore companies unrelated to the business, frequent restructuring
Financial pressure elsewhere in the promoter group
News, credit rating reports, other listed group companies
No material group debt outside the listed company
Heavy unlisted group debt, defaults, or pledges across group companies
How control has changed
Preferential issue notices, warrant disclosures, reclassification filings
No cheap stake increases; changes put to shareholders
Warrants or preferential shares to promoters at floor prices after a fall, avoiding an open offer

children.text: Section B: Board and Audit (Checks 6 to 10)

cells: Board composition against LODR requirements
Corporate Governance Report
Comfortably above the minimum, with a mix of relevant skills
Bare minimum compliance, or periods of non-compliance attracting fines
Real independence of independent directors
Director profiles, AGM notices, attendance tables
Relevant expertise, reasonable tenure, high attendance, no group ties
Long tenures, seats across several group companies, past employment or fee relationships, poor attendance
Audit committee strength
Corporate Governance Report
Chaired by a finance expert, fully independent, meets often
Committee dominated by the weakest directors, or a former company executive chairing it
Audit opinion, Key Audit Matters, and CARO remarks
Independent Auditor's Report and CARO annexure
Unmodified opinion, clean CARO, Key Audit Matters that fit the business
Qualification, going concern uncertainty, or adverse CARO remarks on loans, dues, or defaults
Auditor changes and fees
Exchange announcements; payments to auditors note
Scheduled rotation to a firm of similar standing
Mid-term resignation, a much smaller replacement firm, or large non-audit fees

children.text: Section C: Cash Reaching Insiders (Checks 11 to 15)

cells: Managerial pay against profit, peers, and the median employee
Corporate Governance Report; Board's Report
Modest share of profit, variable pay linked to targets, pay tracking results
Pay growing far faster than profit, several family members on the payroll, pay from subsidiaries
Related party purchases and sales as a share of the business
Related party note; half-yearly RPT filings
Small, stable, mostly with wholly owned subsidiaries
Rising share of revenue or purchases through promoter entities, with slow collections
Related party loans, deposits, and guarantees against net worth
Related party note; CARO 3(iii); contingent liabilities
None outside wholly owned subsidiaries
Loans with no repayment terms, interest accrued but not received, or guarantees for promoter firms
Royalty and brand fees to a parent or group holding company
Related party note; AGM notices
No royalty, or a stable rate with a profit-linked cap
Rate creeping up with no new technology or products, growing faster than profit
Cash returned to shareholders, and where idle cash sits
Cash flow statement; investments note; capital allocation policy
Payout tracks free cash flow, with a written policy that is followed
Cash piling up with no plan, or cash that is actually deposits with group companies

children.text: Section D: Stewardship, Numbers and Conduct (Checks 16 to 20)

cells: Incremental ROCE and value created per rupee retained
screener.in; ten years of financials
New capital earning at or above the existing return; over a rupee of value per rupee retained
Incremental ROCE far below the historical rate, with a falling ROCE trend
Acquisition and diversification record
Annual reports; goodwill and impairment notes
Bolt-on deals in the core business that earned back their price
Large debt-funded or unrelated bets, pet projects, repeated write-offs
Earnings quality
Cash flow statement; accounting policies; working capital days
Cash conversion high and stable, conservative policies, no recurring exceptional items
Profit rising while cash conversion falls, long-lived capital work in progress, exceptional items most years
Guidance versus delivery, and use of money raised
Concalls and presentations; statement of deviation
Targets met or misses explained; issue proceeds used as promised
Repeated misses with the same excuse, targets quietly dropped, unspent or redirected issue proceeds
Regulatory footprint and shareholder votes
SEBI orders; exchange penalties; secretarial audit; voting results
Clean record, strong institutional support at AGMs
Repeated penalties, orders naming promoters, heavy institutional votes against

body.text: Twenty checks sounds heavy. In practice a first pass takes 45 to 60 minutes per company, because seven of the twenty are visible on screener.in alone and another six sit in two documents: the annual report and the latest shareholding pattern. After the first pass, an annual refresh takes 20 minutes, plus an immediate re-check whenever an auditor resigns, a preferential issue is announced, or a regulator acts.

children.text: What a Completed Scorecard Looks Like

body.title: Section scores for two illustrative companies (10 points per section)

children.text: Company A totals 34 out of 40, comfortably in the strong band. Company B totals 13, below the avoid threshold, and its weakest section is C, which is where cash actually leaves a company. Section scores matter as much as the total: a company that loses most of its points in Section C is leaking value, while one that loses them in Section D may simply be a poor capital allocator. Those are different problems with different remedies, and only one of them is likely to be dishonest.

body.title: Add Up the Scorecard
body.prompt: You score a company 7 on Section A, 6 on Section B, 5 on Section C, and 6 on Section D. What is the total out of 40?
body.explanation: 7 + 6 + 5 + 6 = 24, which sits at the bottom of the acceptable band. The score alone does not decide anything: check first that no red line has been crossed, then list the specific items that scored 0 and decide whether each is monitorable or fatal. A 24 made of evenly mixed scores is very different from a 24 with three zeroes in Section C.

body.title: Using the Checklist Well vs Badly

columns.label: Used Well
points: Same 20 checks for every company, including ones you already own
One line of evidence and a document reference for each score
Scores compared with two listed peers, not judged in isolation
Red lines applied before the total is even calculated
Rescored on events, not only once a year

columns.label: Used Badly
points: Scoring generously because you like the business or already hold it
Treating the total as a target price input rather than a risk filter
Ignoring a red line because the other 19 items look fine
Scoring from memory or from brokerage notes instead of filings
Never revisiting the score after the first purchase

body.title: Which Finding Overrides the Total?
body.question: A company scores 33 out of 40 on your checklist. Which single finding should still stop you from investing?
options: Promoter holding fell from 58% to 54% through one disclosed block deal
The statutory auditor resigned mid-term stating that it had not been provided with evidence for balances with certain parties
Managerial remuneration rose 14% in a year when profit rose 9%
The company paid an exchange fine for filing its shareholding pattern four days late
body.explanation: An auditor leaving because it could not get evidence is a red line, because it means the numbers underlying the other 19 checks cannot be relied upon. A single explained block deal, a modest pay increase ahead of profit, and one late filing are all ordinary findings that belong in the scoring, not above it.

body.title: Two Stocks, One Valuation
body.scenario: Two mid cap auto ancillary companies both trade at 18 times earnings with similar growth, margins, and customers. Company P scores 35 on your checklist, with its only zeroes on check 16, incremental ROCE, because a recent capacity expansion has not yet ramped up. Company Q scores 22, with zeroes on check 2 (pledge up from 9% to 34%), check 13 (related party deposits of ₹280 crore against net worth of ₹1,500 crore), check 18 (cash conversion down from 0.8 to 0.4) and check 20 (two SEBI orders on delayed disclosures naming the promoters).
body.prompt: Both are equally priced. What do you do, and what would make you revisit Company Q?
body.modelAnswer: At the same multiple, the choice is straightforward: buy P and not Q, because you are paying the same price for very different risk. P's single weakness is operational and self-correcting if the new capacity ramps up, and it is measurable next year through incremental ROCE. Q's weaknesses interlock in the pattern this course has shown repeatedly: a rising pledge signals promoter cash needs, ₹280 crore of related party deposits, about 19% of net worth, shows where company cash is going, falling cash conversion suggests the reported profit is not arriving in the bank, and regulatory orders on disclosure show the promoters are not forthcoming. None of these is a red line on its own, but together they describe a company whose reported numbers deserve a discount, so 18 times earnings is not the same price at all. You would revisit Q if the deposits were repaid in cash and confirmed in the related party note, the pledge fell back towards zero, cash conversion recovered above 0.7 for two consecutive years, and no new regulatory action appeared. That is a specific, checkable list, which is exactly what a scorecard is for.

body.title: Score Your Largest Holding Today
steps: Open screener.in and the latest annual report, and set aside one hour
Work through Sections A to D in order, scoring each check 0, 1, or 2 with one line of evidence and its source
Before totalling, check the five red lines; if any is crossed, stop and act on that alone
Total the score, note the band, and list every item that scored 0
Repeat for one listed peer so you have a comparison rather than an absolute judgement
Diarise an annual rescore, and set alerts for auditor changes, preferential issues, and regulatory announcements
Keep the sheet; next year's version tells you whether governance is improving or deteriorating

body.text: This checklist is an educational framework, not investment advice or a rating methodology. Scores and bands are judgement tools, and you should verify every input against original filings before acting. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

points: Twenty checks in four sections turn the whole course into one repeatable process: ownership and control, board and audit, cash reaching insiders, and stewardship and conduct
Score each check 0, 1, or 2 out of a maximum of 40; 32 and above is strong, 24 to 31 acceptable with monitoring, 16 to 23 weak, below 16 avoid

Five red lines override the total: adverse or disclaimer opinions, an auditor resigning for lack of evidence, orders restraining promoters, related party exposure above 25% of net worth, and a rising pledge above half the promoter holding
Section scores matter as much as the total, because weakness in Section C means value is leaking while weakness in Section D usually means poor capital allocation
A first pass takes about an hour per company, an annual refresh about 20 minutes, plus event-driven rechecks
Always score a peer alongside, record the evidence and its source, and apply the same standard to stocks you already own
